segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, we have other stories of people who are so close, but so far. Act 1 is about two people in one of the closest relationships possible. They're engaged to be married. But they have this distance between them that they cannot make sense of.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, Love and Other Exports. How much can you trust whether somebody who you think is close to you really is close to you? Saidu Tejan-Thomas Jr. has been thinking about that question since visiting with some of his childhood friends. Saidu was born in Sierra Leone, but moved to the States when he was little. His story starts in Freetown during a recent trip home. Heads up, this story acknowledges the existence of sex.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: When I left Sierra Leone at eight years old, I left behind a small group of friends I did everything with. As kids, we would run around the city and play soccer at the beach. That's how we bonded. Now that we're grown when I go back, we go to the gym. It's how we pick up where we left off.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: [GRUNTING]

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: My friends have this one particular gym they like. It's called Sonics.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: 1, 2, 3, and 4, 5, more, 6, more, 7.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Sonics sits at the end of a dirt road in Freetown, a small space in a quaint green and yellow building. It has no air conditioning and relentless heat. So the guys are usually drenched in sweat like oiled-up extras in '90s R&B videos. I come here almost every time I'm in Salone.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: But then the last time we went, I discovered that for many of the guys here, all their crunches and squats had a much deeper purpose than looking good. The gym, my friends told me, possesses a special luck for young Sierra Leonean men who want to move to America or Europe.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: They believe that if you use the weights here to sculpt your body, make it beautiful enough, you will find a wife overseas, and that Sonics has a track record to prove it. A member named Savage told me about how foolproof this method has been for previous members. He's speaking in Krio. I'll paraphrase after.

segments.text: We not ever get a situation where we get member, we meet with JC, then they normally come up together.

segments.text: Another member of Sonics, this guy with perfectly sculpted arms called Sultan, jumped in to name their legends, the guys they've heard found wives overseas, success stories that get passed around at the gym.

segments.speaker: Sultan

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: There was a driver who chauffeured a Black American woman around Freetown while she was visiting, always making sure to look presentable doing it. He made a good impression. They got married. And he just went to America a few months ago.

segments.text: There was the handsome photographer who got a random phone call from a Sierra Leonean woman living in London. It was a wrong number but he charmed his way into a conversation, sent her some photos of his biceps, and they got married last year. He's now living with her in London.

segments.text: I respected the hustle. But their plans somehow didn't sit right with me. The idea of guys I grew up with, men in my country using their bodies to get overseas, it made me uncomfortable. But then I sat down with a few of the guys and we started to talk. And I realized beneath the surface, beyond all the muscles, confidence, and bravado, all of these men were carrying around a broken heart, which brings me to the guy I wanted to talk to the most, my friend Mark.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: MC Mark, Mario Mark, Mario Mark.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: (SINGING) How do I breathe? How do I breathe?

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Mark and I grew up in the same neighborhood. But we didn't really get to know each other until we were grown. He's a good-looking guy who's easy to talk to. Not the greatest singer, but we were hanging out one day and he decided to sing me his favorite love song.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: (SINGING) --feels so different being here. I was so used to being next to you. Life for me is not the same. There is no one to talk to.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Mario's "How Do I Breathe," one of my favorite songs, is a song about a guy trying to piece together his emotional life after losing the woman he loves. It's basically Mark's story. It's why he's the one of my friends who believes most fervently that finding love overseas is the way to go. The girl he's singing about is someone he grew up with. Mark says she was the smartest kid in their fifth grade class. But she was always approachable. And he liked that. He liked that they could joke together.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: After lessons, they would go to the beach and talk for hours, getting to know each other. He says she was the first person who taught him how to love. Like this one day, he walked home from prayers and as soon as he opened the door, he saw her standing there with all his best friends from school, his family, everyone, singing.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Neither of them came from money, far from it. But Mark was growing up with a single parent. When his mother couldn't afford to care for him, he lived with his grandpa.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: But then his grandpa died. Then his mother died. And Mark became an orphan. He says his relationship with this woman was one of the few things in his life that felt stable. With her, he could dream. He could escape into one of their long talks about how sweet their lives would be in the future.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I reached out to her to get her side of this, but she didn't want to be involved with my story and she wouldn't confirm anything Mark said. The way Mark tells it though, they had decided-- she would work in the energy industry. He would become a lawyer.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: They wanted three to four kids, a house in Salone. Maybe they'd travel sometimes. I love the way he describes the love he had for her.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: So real to me, no...

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: She was so real to me.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: If I get or not get, e nor wan know how i dae or how i look lek, na love e bin get for me.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: She didn't care if I had money or didn't have money. She didn't care how I looked. It's love she had for me.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: True love from the bottom of her heart.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: And you thought to yourself, this is going to be my wife.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yeah, she's going to be my wife in the future since then.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: After they graduated high school, she got a scholarship to attend university abroad. Mark says she tried to put in a good word for him to get the same scholarship, but it didn't work out. Still, he encouraged her to go. And for three years, they continued their relationship via WhatsApp and Facebook. She told him she was one of the top students in her class.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Back home, Mark was struggling. He had no money, no parents, no connections in a country with no reliable jobs for young people. His dreams of becoming a lawyer were fading. But word of his girlfriend's success was starting to get around the wider Sierra Leonean community. Guys were sliding into her DMs on socials. And whenever that happened, she would tell Mark and then block them immediately, until someone new approached her.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: One time when I was sitting down, she told me that I have this guy.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: The guy was a Sierra Leonean doctor. He had seen one picture of Mark's girlfriend and decided that she would be his wife. Mark says she tried to ignore him, but the man contacted her family and formally asked for her hand. She told Mark they were pressuring her to accept, telling her that a marriage with this man could not only change her future, but her entire family's too.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: He watched as the nine years of their relationship unraveled over a short series of tearful WhatsApp calls. Nothing Mark could say, nothing he could do, nothing he could offer her or her family was enough to convince them to choose him over a doctor. A few months later, he says she received the ring via DHL and was married to this stranger.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: A doctor who don't know where you are from, who doesn't know [SUCKS TEETH]. After all the plans, after all the promises, disappointment.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Love became disappointment?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yes, it changes everything because she met somebody, a doctor. The moment will hurt me the most in my life.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: The visionary feminist writer bell hooks says love is made up of seven parts. Wherever someone is practicing care, affection, recognition, respect, commitment, trust, and open, honest communication, there is love, even in an economically poor environment like Salone. But talking to Mark, I found myself thinking more about what love needs to survive, what conditions can make the act of loving easier or more difficult to sustain. Mark felt like he couldn't compete because of money. And he was right. Not everyone has equal access to love.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: I feel like crying. But it's shameful to cry before you. [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: You feel like crying, but you're ashamed to cry in front of me? You should cry!

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: I miss those moments with her.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: In the years since I left Salone, I had fantasies about the lives of people back home. Our country had been ravaged by years of war that left a lot of heartache, suffering, and poverty in its wake. But I believe that through all of that, people had each other, that they had this unbreakable bond that was vital to our survival. But Mark was telling me that was wrong.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: I don't think-- love is not here. If it is, it's at 10% or 5%.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: If it is, only 10% or 5% have true love. It wasn't just Mark. Almost every guy I talked to in Freetown told me the same thing. It felt like there was this lovelessness among the men in Salone. Every time I raised a question-- and I talked to around 18 or 19 people-- they'd launch into their own stories of heartbreak.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I heard it from the taxi drivers, coconut salesmen, hotel bellhops, random guys on the street-- women too. The guys at Sonics gym said they'd all gone through it and independently landed on the same math. I asked them what percent of people without money in Salone find true love.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: What's the percent of true love without money in Salone?

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: I say, yeah, sure.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: When I ask my friends in America the same question about finding love without money, they say 60% to 80%.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: If love was like everything else these guys couldn't afford in Salone, if it really was a luxury, it made sense to me that they thought the best course of action was to look for it abroad.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: It was a way to solve two problems at once. They could move to a country where poverty was less rampant and true love was more accessible. But I wondered about it. Where would it lead them? For Mark, it led him to the place most of us turn to for finding love these days, the internet.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: It makes me feel good, like, talking to someone that is far away from me, like someone that is in America, you-- it would make me feel like-- I would just close my eyes. I feel like I'm in America.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Listening to Mark, it was like I was watching an episode of 90 Day Fiancé, but seeing the side of the story I'd always wanted to see, the version where the hopes and dreams of the foreign spouse were finally center stage. My friend Mark was eagerly searching for a love that could transform his life. He made a few connections, but most women weren't interested in a long distance relationship with a guy all the way in West Africa. So Mark struck out again and again.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Lottie Rebecca Beasley was a Black woman Mark met through Facebook. And he just loved how regal her name sounded, Lottie Rebecca Beasley. You've got to say all three. She had kind eyes, a warm smile, and she lived in this state that Mark had never heard of.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Fairbanks, Alaska, in the morning there, here it's midnight. 1:00, 2:00, 3:00 AM in the morning, I usually wake up just to talk to Lottie until 5:00 or 6:00 AM. It's all in the morning hours.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: But the nine hour time difference wasn't the only obstacle. There was another distance too.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: She was born on 1949. She just turned 73 years of age this past September.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: And did you know that before you clicked on her profile?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: A 70-year-old woman wasn't what Mark expected. Most of the guys at the gym who had been successful had ended up with wives closer to their own age. But while Mark had been casting a wide net in search of a relationship that could change his life, he was also open to meeting a new friend. So he didn't overthink the age thing with Lottie. And she was calm about it too. In her very first message, she roasted him about how young he was.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: They jusy say hey, who are you, little boy? Who are you, little boy? What do you want? I said, I'm not a little boy. I'm a man.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: How old were you when you met her?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: 21 or, 22, yeah, 21 or 22.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Mark was young, but he's a good listener. Before long, Lottie was telling him all about her life. She'd gone through a lot of heartbreak too. She'd been married three times, had five children. And after one of her husbands had become abusive, she needed to get away. That's how she ended up in Alaska. She made the best of it, started her own business caring for the elderly, and was moving on with her life. She wanted to know about Mark too.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: What about my life? How I lost my father, I lost my mother. She said, oh, you're an orphan? I said, yes. She was having this sympathy for me. She was feeling sorry for me.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: For Mark, this thing that began as a friendship was starting to grow. He saw a potential for a romantic relationship. But Lottie struggled to see it, even though he felt like she wanted to. The age difference was too much. Mark says most people feel that way.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: So when you tell-- whenever you tell people about Lottie, about your relationship with this--

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Don't believe. Don't believe. They all say, this is scam, this is scam. It's normal, though. People get their own thoughts and get their own thinking. And life, people must talk anything you do in this life. So if you live, if you stop by to listen to everyone, every word they say towards you, trust me, you won't even achieve your goal. Sometimes I'll give them deaf ears.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I got to say, when Mark first told me about Lottie, I had questions too. Like I wondered, was my friend now a bona fide romance scammer or something? Because it is true that the way that he was looking for love gave him the silhouette of a romance scammer.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Scammers ask people questions about their personal life, send sweet messages. They try to earn trust before stealing your money and disappearing. But what Mark was telling me about his relationship made me believe that this wasn't that. Mark never asked for money. And he was putting in a lot of time with Lottie.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: When she was in the hospital, day and night, I check on her. I said, I'm here. We're far in distance, but you are close to my heart. I said, I'm here praying for you day and night.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: She had to accept me. Because of the way I talk to her, the way I care about her, do I call her when I woke up-- I wake up from sleep. I check on her. How are you doing? How's your health now?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Months passed and Mark and Lottie kept talking, developing a love ethic where they both showed up for each other.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: At one point, she actually said, did you eat breakfast this morning?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Did you breakfast this morning?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: I said, what is breakfast. [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: And I said, what is breakfast?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: I said, OK. I said, no. I said, no. I said, please. I said, just understand. Here in Africa, our breakfast is for the politicians-- for the presidents, politicians, first lady. I said, sometimes when I wake up in the morning, I don't even taste food 'til 12:00 PM or 3 o'clock, sometimes even in the evening hours.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Lottie asked about where Mark stayed. And he told her he shared one room with three other people. And most nights, he would have to stand outside the house to talk to her so he wouldn't disturb his roommates. This is common. Most people in Salone live on roughly $2 a day. Mark had been making a little money playing soccer in some local leagues, but it wasn't enough to get by.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Hearing about how Mark was struggling made Lottie upset. So she decided to start sending him money. $200 covered rent for the entire year at a place all his own. She also paid for his grandma's funeral. It wasn't a huge amount, just what she could spare here and there, but it made her feel happy to help him.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: So when she used to call me, Mark. I said, yeah, Lottie, yes, sweetheart. She said, did you eat breakfast? Yeah. Now is the time to have breakfast. Just laughing, ah, Lottie. When I close my eyes. I just think like she's in front of me.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: What do you think you were providing her? What do you think you were giving her? How were you contributing to the relationship?

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Because she's contributing money. And she's contributing like financially. So what do you think you were contributing to the relationship?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Love, love and caring for her.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I can see that. A lot of relationships involve some kind of transaction. Each person brings what they can offer to the mix. With Lottie, it's money, at least partly. And with Mark, it's his time and care. When I think about the contours of their relationship, the fact that they've never met in person and live thousands of miles apart, not to mention the difference in age and experience, it makes me a little uneasy.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: So did you guys talk about sex? Do you talk about sex ever?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Everything, we talk about sex, talk about everything.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: So how did that-- how does that-- if you don't mind me asking, so how do you--

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: We make sex on the phone.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: You guys had phone sex?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Phone sex. Like we will talk when lying down. Climb onto my chest. OK. Are you there? Can I put something there? OK.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Let me ask you this question, actually. Are you attracted to her?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: What about her are you attracted to? What turns you on about her?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Even she's 73 years old, she still love back. Her back is set just like Nicki Minaj. OK, Nicki Minaj is-- [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: OK, so you think when you and her meet in person, you'll have no issue having sex with her?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: I have no issue. What?

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: If I'm being real, my worry for Mark isn't just about whether or not he's attracted to Lottie. There's a darker place my mind wanders off to. It's hard not to see their relationship in the context of the exploitation that's happening in West Africa right now. Sexual tourism has been a growing problem in the Gambia, for example.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Older women have been descending on the country and spending their money on sex with young African men. The phenomenon is so rampant that the Gambian government stepped in, demanding foreign visitors stop this practice. But it still continues.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I don't think that's what's happening with Mark and Lottie. But there are enough similarities here to make me question. And if half of me worried that my friend was being taken advantage of, the other half worried for Lottie. Because Mark talked so openly about what he hopes to get out of their relationship.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: What did you like about her? What did you feel?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: You remember I told you earlier that I want to accomplish my dream. I want to go to the United States or Europe.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: That's not feelings you have for her. That's feelings you have for your dream. Those are two different things.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yeah, if she's going-- if she's the one who's going to take me from here, then.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Then the feelings for your dreams become your feelings for her?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: I've already said, Lottie, if you take me out of here, trust me, no matter the age difference, I swear to my life, we'll be together 'til God sends one home.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: So you told her, you told her, if you take me out of here, I will love you forever, basically. So she knows that you, there's something that you want. She knows that there's something that you want beyond her.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yes, sure.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I'd been reaching out to Lottie for weeks with no luck to get her side of all of this. Then finally, early one morning, around 3:00 AM.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: She called me back. And we talked for a while. I didn't know what to expect. But Lottie was very open about her life. She told me more about her work caring for the elderly, the grandson who put her up in her own apartment when she got older, and then, of course, we talked about her feelings for Mark.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: I love Mark. I can't even understand how I fell in love with Mark. Because I ain't never dealt with no young man. I was just talking to him as a friend.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Lottie can be a little hard to understand sometimes. It's because of a botched intubation she went through years ago. But I have to say, despite that, she doesn't come off as the kind of person who doesn't have agency over her life. At 73, she can clearly hold her own.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: And I don't let nothing stop me. Do you see my picture on Facebook?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, I've seen it.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: Do I look like I'm 73 years old?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: My mother definitely taught me better than to comment on a woman's age. But I will say, in Lottie's profile picture, she has a very youthful energy about her. In our conversation, she confirmed all of what Mark said about their relationship and how intense their connection was from the start.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: I've never experienced anything like this. I mean, I've talked to-- I talk to him sometimes 50 times a day.

segments.speaker: Saidu   Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Wow. When you and Mark met in that first year or so, what was going on in your life?

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: I was sad. You know, I wasn't happy. I was lonely. And from talking to him, that's how my heart grew to him. We talk about life together. I have dreamed sometimes of me and Mark, Mark coming in the house one day and how happy I was.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: So you feel like he loves you for who you are?

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Lottie said that it had been a while since men her age gave her a chance. It had been more than 10 years since her previous relationship. And with Mark, she felt like she'd found something real. But some of the things she told me about her life were head spinning.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: She told me about a violent fight with one of her adult kids and how, in a separate incident in 2002, she was convicted of child abuse and was sentenced to 2 and 1/2 years in prison. It made me worry for Mark a little bit. Like, does he really know this person?

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: When I told him about what Lottie had said, he told me he wasn't aware of any of that stuff. But he didn't find that alarming. He said, after all the good she's done for him, he's not going to turn his back on her now.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: After six months of a long distance relationship and countless marathon phone sessions, Mark got what he was looking for. Lottie agreed to marry him. The initial plan was for her to go to Salone, but her doctors told her the travel would be bad for her health. So, instead, they decided to bring Mark to the States. Here's Mark.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: She even bought the ring, bought everything, my suit, everything for the wedding. She even chose the-- my best man. She already choosing him from the church. Yes, everyone was waiting for them to witness this marriage.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Mark went ahead and applied for a visitor's visa to the US. And Lottie wrote an official letter to the US embassy in Salone inviting him to come. Next up was an interview with a woman at the American embassy. She said to him--

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: What is your name? I show her my name. And who is this to you? I said, she is my lover.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: The interviewer asked a lot of questions, carefully grilling him about every detail of his plan. Mark was nervous, but he was prepared. He knew Lottie's address by heart. He felt like he'd answered every question right, until the end when the interviewer looked up at him.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: She said, well, I'm sorry, better luck next time.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: She said that? She said, "better luck next time?"

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. I cannot issue this visa. Better luck next time.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Wow, how did you-- what did you say back?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: It was like tears started falling down my eyes.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Oh, you started crying right there?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yeah, I started crying right there at the embassy.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I wasn't surprised that Mark didn't get it. It's always hard for someone like Mark, someone without a job or a house to tie them to their home country, to get a visitor's visa to America. Officials are afraid that people like that, basically poor people, won't have a reason to return.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: It's messed up. And I feel for Mark. In an instant, all the physical and emotional labor he'd invested to get to this point was wiped away, erased by a stranger behind a desk. I've known a lot of folks in Salone who've been denied a visa. And Mark responded to his rejection the way they all eventually do, with optimism. Because what other choice is there in a situation like this?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: That is the happiest moment for me.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Right. Because it was like an official thing. It was very official.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Yeah, for me to go to the-- walk into American embassy. Wow, American Embassy, for an interview. Wow, even when they don't issue me visa, I'm sad about that. I'm not happy. It hurts me. But at the same time, I'm happy because I went there for an interview.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Because you got to touch a piece of America?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: It's really, really a blessing to me.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: After the failed interview at the embassy, Mark and Lottie tried to regroup and come up with a different plan. But her health worsened. Then one day last year, Lottie didn't answer the phone when Mark called. For weeks, he couldn't reach her, until finally, she messaged him on Facebook.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: She told him she'd been in the hospital. At one point, her heart stopped. It took them eight minutes to revive her. Once she got out of the hospital, Mark says, she was more isolated than before and her life felt more difficult.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Things are really hard for her. Because she's all alone in the house. People don't come to help. Sometimes I shed tears for her. It is really paining me. I pray five times a day. And every day I pray for Lottie Rebecca Beasley.

segments.speaker: Saidu   Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Talking to Mark, I can tell that he's genuinely troubled by what Lottie's been going through. It's also true that since the downturn in her health, his circumstances have gotten worse. He says without the money she was sending, he got evicted.

segments.speaker: Saidu   Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: He doesn't always have money for food. But he insists even though Lottie has stopped supporting him, he still feels responsible for her.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: When she was supporting me, when she was, she was OK, she was not sick, and now if she's like in this difficult time she is not even walking, I think I should be with her too and that's my duty to look after her. The love does not stop because I love her. Because I have all allegiance to her. I love her. I really love the relationship. So I love her.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: The way Mark is talking about Lottie here, it reminds me of a business person talking about sunk costs, someone who is reluctant to give up on something they've invested in for a long time. It brings me right back to my initial worry. What does Mark actually feel? And what is he convincing himself he feels?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: There's a part of me that believes you. But then there's a part of me that's still like, this doesn't-- this makes-- this doesn't look, this doesn't look right. It doesn't feel right.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: It literally, it looks like-- yeah, it looks like you're using her and she's using you. It looks like she's lonely and she wants somebody to talk to. So she's using you for that. And you don't have money.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: And you need somebody to fund you and take you out of this place. So you're using her for that. It looks like you guys are mutually using each other. And, yeah, you guys love each other. You could very much love each other through that.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: But it still looks very obvious to me what's happening here. It looks very, look very clear to me that [SPEAKING KRIO]. And I just want to know, I just want to know what you think about that and what you think about me saying that.

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: Nobody is not using anyone between me and Lottie. How many people are there in the United States?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Billions?

segments.speaker: Mark
segments.text: OK, billions, yeah, there are billions of people, but no one sees me here. Only Lottie who is 73 years old woman sees me. It's really a blessing for me, so.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: The US population is actually in the millions, but you get the point. When I talked to Lottie, she also seemed to question how to think about the relationship.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: You know him very well, right?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: Do you think he loves me?

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Do I think he loves you?

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I got the sense that a lot of people in her life have asked her the same thing for years. And, honestly, it was a hard question to answer.

segments.speaker: Saidu  Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I think Mark loves you the way you love him, if that makes sense.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: It didn't make sense. So later, she asked me again.

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: Do you think Mark really loves me?

segments.speaker: Saidu      Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: I've asked him the same question, Lottie. I've asked him the same question up, left, down, right, and center and he says, "yes." And I'm not going to be-- I'm not going to lie to you. I didn't believe him either because of the age difference, because of the cultural difference, because of the distance. So I didn't believe him.

segments.speaker: Saidu      Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: But he keeps saying "yes." He keeps saying, he swears up and down that he loves you. So I kind of have no choice but to believe him. Do you think he loves you?

segments.speaker: Lottie
segments.text: I feel he loves me. In my heart, I feel he loves me.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Ultimately, I don't think it's my place to decide whether or not two people love each other. That's a call only they get to make, the way everyone else gets to. But I do know both Mark and Lottie have been through plenty of heartbreak. And I know heartbreak is just love without a place to call home.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: The fact that two Black people were struggling to find that home on damn near opposite ends of the Earth, both from two vastly different cultures and generations, says a lot about how hard it can be for Black folks to love and be loved in this world. For us, there's a whole host of historical, political, and economic forces that can send our search for partnership down wayward paths. And after years of wandering, Mark and Lottie felt like they'd finally landed on something. But what I want for them is what I want for a lot of us-- ease.

segments.speaker: Saidu Tejan-Thomas
segments.text: Mark deserves to be in a relationship that's free from people's judgment. Maybe that comes with a partner closer to his age, in Salone or in America. And Lottie deserves a relationship where she doesn't have to worry about whether someone's using her and whether she's loved. What they have now is not simple. It's not easy. But then again, when has love ever been that?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Saidu Tejan-Thomas Jr. is the host of the podcast Resistance. This story was produced by Alix Spiegel.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, Tig Notaro, then a love that dare not speak its name. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, So Close and Yet So Far, stories of people who feel so near to each other, and yet are kept apart.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And before we move to Act 2, we heard about one instance of this kind of thing in a story Jake Offenhartz did on the website Gothamist. Basically what happened is, a few days ago, the New York City fire department received this emergency call.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: What's the address you sent in?

segments.speaker: Kid

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: You don't know?

segments.speaker: Kid

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: You're stuck where?

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: In the sewers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the sewers. Five kids, Staten Island. You know, a normal Tuesday night.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: How did you guys get in there?

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: We went through the tunnels.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They went through the tunnels. The dispatcher hands over the call to another dispatcher, Marlind Haxhialiu.

segments.speaker: Marlind Haxhialiu
segments.text: HEY DID YOU GUYS GO IN FROM BROADWAY OR MARTLING, THE MAIN ENTRANCE?

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: It's like Clove Lake.

segments.speaker: Marlind Haxhialiu
segments.text: WHERE? IN THE PARKING LOT?

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: No no, you know where the cemetery is?

segments.speaker: Marlind Haxhialiu
segments.text: OKAY I KNOW THE CEMETERY, ACROSS THE STREET, YEAH.

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira  Glass
segments.text: Can we just step back and admire this dispatcher who seems to know every sewer entrance on Staten Island.

segments.speaker: Marlind Haxhialiu
segments.text: Okay, but what do you mean by a sewer? Is it like a grate?

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: It's like a tunnel where all the pipes are.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's like a tunnel where all the pipes are.

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: We crawled. It's like a tunnel kinda.

segments.speaker: Marlind Haxhialiu
segments.text: Listen to me. I know the area, listen to me. Hey, I know the area very well. I'm trying to ask you, how did you get to the sewer? You walked through the cemetery, right? Did you go right or left at the end of the cemetery? I need you to guide me.

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: No, we went down.

segments.speaker: Marlind Haxhialiu
segments.text: You went down. Okay.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Very quickly, they figure out where the kids are.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Stay on the line. I'm gonna get you some help, okay?

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: I hear sirens.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Wait, hang on.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: [SIRENS]

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: I hear the sirens.

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: [SIRENS]

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: It sounded like it went past us.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Hold on. We're gonna get to you. Now you can scream as loud as you can. They want you to scream and yell. They can hear you, so scream.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: These kids, it's like they went through a trapdoor from regular New York to underground New York. Which is going on all the time, of course, under the city. Sewers and tunnels and water mains. Literally just shouting distance away. And shouting is all it'll take now for them to tap their ruby slippers three times and get home.

segments.speaker: Kid
segments.text: Scream?

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Call for help, guys. They hear you. Call for help.

segments.speaker: Multiple Kids
segments.text: [SCREAMS] Ahhh!! Ahhhh!!!! Ahhhhhh!!! Ahhh!!!!!!!

segments.speaker: Ira   Glass
segments.text: If you listen very closely it sounds like one of the kids actually laughs a little on that last scream, like, it is so weird that an adult is asking them to do this. The kids were rescued pretty quickly. None of them were hurt.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Keep screaming guys, keep screaming. I want you guys to scream as loud as you want.

segments.speaker: Multiple  Kids
segments.text: [SCREAMS] Ahhh!!! Ahhhh!!!!! Ahhhh!!!!!! Ahhhh!!!!!! Help!!!!! Help!!!!!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which brings us to Act 2 where we have another kind of rescue. Another fire department. Act 2-- Fire Sale.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So comedian Tig Notaro has been on our show many, many times talking about her random encounters with pop star Taylor Dayne or, memorably, she was diagnosed with stage II cancer and went up on stage that night and did a stand up set about it that we played here on the show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Lately, when she goes on stage, she's been talking a lot about her wife Stephanie and their two kids, Finn and Max, and their home life together. And she has this story of being so close to someone and yet so far from them that she recorded at the Comedy Club Largo in Los Angeles. This happened one night when she and Stephanie went to a film and got home late.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: She fell asleep immediately. And I was up. I was having some pain in my stomach. And because she fell asleep right away, I thought, well, I'm not going to wake her up. So I was lying there thinking, I'm sure this is nothing. You know, all of my medical issues usually aren't anything. So this is probably another one of those situations. [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And three hours pass. And I'm am worse and worse. And I finally tapped her and I said, I am in so much pain right now. And she said, completely groggy, just, do you think it's all the popcorn that you ate tonight? And I said, mm, I don't, I don't.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: I've been eating popcorn for almost 50 years now. Not consistently, but this is not popcorn pain. And she said, well, we should probably be safe and just go to the emergency room. And I was like, oh my god, that's so dramatic.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And she said, well, you know, I just-- we shouldn't take any chances. So why don't you get up and get dressed and we'll go? And I said, well, the thing is, I don't know if I can even walk I'm in so much pain. And she said, oh my god, you can't walk? Well, then I'm calling 911. And I was like, oh my god, that's so dramatic. It's going to be the lights and sirens flying down our street.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: What if this is nothing? She calls 9-1-1. And this gigantic fireman appears at our bedroom door. I mean, he's huge. And he has rubber boots to here. He has fireman pants on, muscles out to here, suspenders, no shirt.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And I'm lying there in bed. I felt so vulnerable. Because I was in so much pain. And I'm in my nightgown. And-- of course I don't wear a nightgown. You know me better than that. You think I wear a nightgown? I could feel the tension in the room.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: Are you like, she wears a nightgown? No, I don't wear a nightgown. I think the last time I wore a nightgown was probably 1977, probably had a little Pooh Bear on the front scooping honey out of a clay pot. Anyway, I was lying in bed totally feeling vulnerable.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And he got down next to me and he said, listen, I understand you're in a lot of pain. And I just want you to know that there's an ambulance outside if you need. And I said, I appreciate it. I just really don't want to waste anybody's time if this is nothing. And he said, it's up to you. It's there.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And I said, I don't know if I can walk. And he said, that is not a problem. And he scooped me up in his arms. And I'm telling you, in that moment, I was just like, whoa-ho, I could get used to this. Bada-bing, bada-boom.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: I mean, truly, I was like oh, I get it now. If you think you're surprised, think how I felt in that moment. I have never been more confused. He was holding me and I was just dangling in his arms, with my nightgown flowing.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: But let me tell you what really surprised me when I found out this was my type. Here's what I didn't know I was into. He had a mustache. I was like, yes, please. That'll do just fine. That is my type. I didn't know.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: Here's the thing is you can fall for and be attracted to anybody. It can happen at any time. And I always thought, OK, if I'm ever into a guy, here's what I thought my type would be. I was like, it's probably going to be a singer-songwriter, probably going to be a poet, probably going to be a painter, have a slight build. We'll share a wardrobe. I did not think that this gigantic fireman was going to be what it was all about for me.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: So he's carrying me in his arms. We're going down the hall. And I said, listen, when we pass this door, if you could just be extra quiet because if my kids wake up, come out, and see this, this is going to be confusing on so many different levels. And he was great about it.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: You know how he is. He's just, he's the best, classic him. You know, he's just tiptoeing past their bedroom. We go down the stairs. And Stephanie's father lives with us. And he carries me past my father-in-law. And Stephanie opens the door. And we walk past her. And I just turned and was like, goodbye, old life.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: We get out to the ambulance. He gently places me on the gurney, kisses me on the forehead, and pushes me into the back there and then shuts the doors. And then wouldn't you know it? I was like, oh God, hey, apparently my roommate is worried about me and wants to join us. Thanks a lot, Stephanie. Total buzzkill.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: But as I suspected, it ended up not being anything too serious. I was just bleeding internally. But the couple of weeks later, I was at a party. And I was talking to some people about the fireman. And I was like, this guy was so incredibly hot, just muscles, mustache.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And I was going on and on. Stephanie walks up and overhears this. And she has this look of disgust on her face. And she's like, I'm sorry, but you thought that fireman was hot? I was like, um, yeah. This is not up for discussion.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: This is not a matter of opinion. This is a matter of fact. And I don't know if any of you have experienced this or not. But there is nothing more awkward than finding out in a social situation that you and your wife have completely different tastes in men.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tig Notaro, she is the host of the podcast Don't Ask Tig. She's appearing at Red Bank, New Jersey in April and other places too. To find out when she's coming to your town, her website is TigNotaro.com.
